event: Multiple banks in La Paz closed during protests in Bolivia where demonstrators called for President Rodrigo Paz to resign.

verified_facts.statement: Multiple banks in La Paz closed during protests
verified_facts.source_url: news reports of October 2024 Bolivia protests
verified_facts.note: Bank closures are a documented feature of the blockade period

verified_facts.statement: Demonstrators called for President Rodrigo Paz to resign
verified_facts.note: Resignation demand is a core, widely-reported protest objective

verified_facts.statement: Paz won the 2023 election with approximately 55% of the vote
verified_facts.note: Electoral outcome is a matter of public record

verified_facts.statement: Evo Morales has a fugitive status and arrest warrant
verified_facts.note: Morales fled Bolivia in 2023; warrant status is documented

verified_facts.statement: The DEA returned to Bolivia after an 18-year absence
verified_facts.source_url: DEA and U.S. State Department announcements
verified_facts.note: DEA re-entry is a documented policy shift under Paz

verified_facts.statement: Paz reversed campaign commitments, including on fuel subsidies
verified_facts.source_url: campaign platform vs. policy announcements October 2024
verified_facts.note: Policy reversals are documented in government statements and news

verified_facts.statement: At least 10 people were killed during the protests
verified_facts.source_url: casualty reports from October 2024 Bolivia crisis
verified_facts.note: Death toll is reported across multiple sources; exact attribution varies

verified_facts.statement: Paz signed emergency legislation suspending constitutional rights
verified_facts.note: Emergency decree is a documented government action

verified_facts.statement: Blockades prevented movement of trucks and goods into La Paz
verified_facts.note: Blockade effects on supply chains are widely documented

verified_facts.statement: Inflation was reported in the 14-20% range
verified_facts.note: Inflation figures vary by source and measurement period but cluster in this range

verified_facts.statement: Food, fuel, and medicine shortages occurred in La Paz during the crisis
verified_facts.note: Shortages are widely documented; causation (blockade vs. policy) is disputed

unverified_shared_claims.statement: At least 3 deaths were specifically caused by blocked ambulances
unverified_shared_claims.note: While deaths occurred and ambulance blockades are documented, direct causal attribution to specific deaths requires medical/investigative confirmation not universally available

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Bolivia's economic crisis is 40 years old and rooted in gas reserve depletion
unverified_shared_claims.note: Long-term economic decline is real, but the precise origin date and primary driver (gas reserves vs. other factors) is subject to economic interpretation

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The 2003 Gas War massacre killed 67 people
unverified_shared_claims.note: The 2003 Gas War is historical fact; casualty figures vary in sources (60–67 range reported)

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Morales and drug-trafficking interests are financing the blockades
unverified_shared_claims.note: Paz administration and allies assert this; no independent verification of funding flows has been publicly confirmed

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Protesters used dynamite and Molotov cocktails
unverified_shared_claims.note: Some reports document these tactics; extent and frequency are contested between framings

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The blockades cost Bolivia $50M per day in economic losses
unverified_shared_claims.note: Economic impact estimates vary widely; this figure is cited but not independently verified across sources

points_of_disagreement: Whether the protests represent a genuine mass uprising rooted in economic suffering and Indigenous exclusion (Anti-Austerity framing) vs. an orchestrated destabilization by Morales and narco-interests (Destabilization framing)
Whether Paz's neoliberal reforms and policy reversals are the primary cause of the crisis vs. whether they are a response to structural economic collapse that predates his administration
Whether the blockades constitute a de facto coup attempt undermining democratic order vs. a legitimate exercise of protest rights against an unresponsive government
Whether the humanitarian crisis is primarily caused by protest blockades vs. by government policy failures (fuel subsidies, gasoline imports, economic mismanagement)
Whether Paz's emergency legislation and 'narco-terrorist' labeling represent necessary security measures vs. dangerous escalation and civil liberties violations
Whether U.S. involvement (DEA return, Trump administration backing, geopolitical alignment) represents imperialism and client-state protection vs. legitimate anti-narcotics cooperation
Whether Paz's lack of a legislative majority and governing coalition reflects his incompetence vs. the structural difficulty of governing a fractured parliament
Whether the recall referendum mechanism is a legitimate democratic alternative to blockades vs. an inadequate remedy for urgent grievances
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that multiple banks closed in La Paz during protests demanding Paz's resignation, that at least 10 people died, ~365 were arrested, food/fuel/medicine shortages occurred, and Paz reversed campaign commitments while signing emergency legislation. The disagreement centers on causation (policy failure vs. structural collapse vs. orchestrated destabilization), legitimacy (democratic protest vs. coup attempt), and responsibility for the humanitarian crisis (blockades vs. government policy).

framings.name: Anti-Austerity / Class & Indigenous Exclusion
framings.question: Are these protests a legitimate popular uprising against austerity policies and the political exclusion of Indigenous and working-class Bolivians?
framings.key_claim: Paz's neoliberal reforms — scrapping fuel subsidies, appointing a business-elite cabinet, and ignoring Indigenous communities — have driven a genuine mass uprising rooted in economic suffering and racial exclusion.
framings.description: This framing centers the protests as a bottom-up, multi-sector mobilization by workers, farmers, miners, teachers, and Indigenous communities responding to material hardship and political betrayal. It treats the demonstrations as structurally legitimate regardless of who may be co-opting them.
framings.emphasizes: Inflation at 14-20%, fuel shortages caused by government policy, cabinet packed with business elites, broken campaign promises to Indigenous voters, food and medicine shortages hitting ordinary residents
framings.downplays: Violence by some protesters, Evo Morales's role in organizing marches, potential criminal financing of blockades, economic dysfunction inherited from the MAS era

framings.name: Democratic Destabilization / Narco-Political Coup
framings.question: Are the protests a coordinated, externally directed effort — by Evo Morales and/or drug trafficking networks — to overthrow a legitimately elected democratic government?
framings.key_claim: Evo Morales and criminal drug-trafficking interests, threatened by Paz's DEA partnership and anti-narco policies, are financing and orchestrating the blockades as a de facto coup attempt against Bolivia's democracy.
framings.description: This framing, promoted by the Paz government and echoed by the Trump administration and allied Latin American governments, casts protesters not as independent civic actors but as instruments of criminal and political agendas. It emphasizes state legitimacy and security over grievance.
framings.emphasizes: Morales's fugitive status and arrest warrant, DEA's return after 18-year absence, drug cartel financial interests in Paz's downfall, U.S. and regional bloc statements defending the elected government
framings.downplays: Genuine economic hardship driving protests, absence of evidence for narco-financing, diverse and multi-sector nature of protest coalitions, history of militarized crackdowns toppling Bolivian presidents

framings.name: Human Cost / Humanitarian Crisis
framings.question: Who is being harmed by the blockades and unrest, and what is the measurable toll on ordinary Bolivians?
framings.key_claim: The convergence of protest blockades and state responses has created a humanitarian emergency in La Paz, with shortages of food, fuel, and medicine causing real suffering and death among civilians unrelated to political disputes.
framings.description: This framing focuses on the lived consequences of the standoff — closed banks, empty shelves, oxygen-depleted hospitals, stranded vehicles — and treats the physical siege of La Paz as a crisis affecting all residents regardless of their political sympathies.
framings.emphasizes: Bank closures, food and medicine shortages, hospital oxygen depletion, civilians blocked from emergency services, at least 3 deaths from blocked ambulances, 10 killed overall, 365 arrested
framings.downplays: Root causes of protests, political actors' responsibilities, ideological stakes of the conflict

framings.name: Governance Failure / Presidential Incompetence
framings.question: Has President Paz's own mismanagement, broken promises, and political inexperience created the conditions for this crisis?
framings.key_claim: Paz's failure to build a governing coalition, his reversal of campaign commitments, and his bungled economic policies — including importing 'junk gasoline' — are the proximate cause of a crisis that an effective president could have avoided.
framings.description: This framing assigns primary responsibility not to protesters or external actors but to Paz himself — his weak party infrastructure, politically homogeneous cabinet, and series of policy reversals that compounded public grievance.
framings.emphasizes: Paz's lack of a legislative majority, cabinet reshuffle failures, the 'junk gasoline' scandal, annulling Law 1720 without ending protests, symbolic salary cuts seen as inadequate, flight to Sucre
framings.downplays: Structural economic inheritance from the MAS era, external destabilization pressures, legitimate grievances of protesters

framings.name: Geopolitical Proxy / U.S. Imperialism vs. Regional Left
framings.question: Are the protests and the government's response a theater of U.S.-backed right-wing consolidation against Latin American social movements?
framings.key_claim: Paz's alignment with Trump, the DEA, and regional right-wing coalitions has turned Bolivia into a geopolitical front line, with the U.S. actively characterizing democratic protest as narco-terrorism to protect a client government.
framings.description: This framing reads the Bolivian crisis through the lens of U.S. hemispheric strategy, interpreting Washington's support for Paz — including Hegseth's 'overthrow' statement and the DEA's return — as direct interference in Bolivian self-determination against an Indigenous-majority protest movement.
framings.emphasizes: Trump's 'Shield of the Americas' / A3C coalition, Hegseth's social media intervention, DEA return after 18-year absence, Colombia's ambassador expulsion, Argentina's Milei sending 'humanitarian' police equipment, U.S. Deputy Secretary Landau's backing
framings.downplays: Morales's legal jeopardy and possible manipulation of protests, genuine economic dysfunction created by MAS-era mismanagement, legitimate security interests in coca-producing regions

framings.name: Democratic Order / Rule of Law Under Threat
framings.question: Do the blockades, violence, and demands for forced resignation pose an illegitimate threat to constitutional governance and democratic norms?
framings.key_claim: Regardless of the validity of underlying grievances, the use of indefinite blockades, dynamite, and coordinated siege tactics to force a president from office just seven months after an election undermines democratic institutions and constitutional order.
framings.description: This framing, distinct from the narco-conspiracy frame, emphasizes procedural democracy: elections confer legitimacy, and extra-constitutional pressure — even from genuine popular majorities — threatens the norms that protect all future governments. It often coexists with acknowledgment of real grievances.
framings.emphasizes: Paz's electoral mandate (55% of the vote), constitutional mechanisms for redress, violence by some protesters (dynamite, Molotovs), the recall referendum proposal as the legitimate alternative, historical precedent of protest-toppled Bolivian presidents
framings.downplays: The depth and breadth of public grievance, Paz's own role in provoking the crisis, U.S. support tilting the power balance

framings.name: Economic Crisis / Structural Collapse
framings.question: Are the protests primarily a symptom of a deep, structural economic breakdown that transcends any single government or political actor?
framings.key_claim: Bolivia's protests are the inevitable explosion of a 40-year economic crisis driven by dwindling gas reserves, dollar shortages, and decades of mismanagement that no single administration could resolve in six months.
framings.description: This framing, prominent in financial media and centrist outlets, treats the unrest as a macro-economic story: the protests are rational responses to inflation of 14-20%, fuel subsidy removal, and collapsing foreign reserves — structural problems that predate Paz and would challenge any government.
framings.emphasizes: Forty-year economic lows, 14% inflation, $50M/day economic loss from blockades, 5,000 trucks stranded, foreign reserve depletion, MAS-era economic mismanagement as the structural origin
framings.downplays: Political agency of specific actors, Indigenous rights dimensions, U.S. geopolitical involvement, Paz's role in worsening the crisis

framings.name: Use-of-Force / Civil Liberties
framings.question: Is the government's response — emergency legislation, potential military deployment, mass arrests, and narco-terrorist labeling — a disproportionate threat to civil liberties and constitutional rights?
framings.key_claim: Paz's decision to sign emergency legislation suspending constitutional rights and adopt the Trump administration's 'narco-terrorist' label for largely peaceful protesters represents a dangerous escalation that could repeat Bolivia's history of brutal state violence.
framings.description: This framing scrutinizes the government's tools of response rather than the protests themselves, asking whether the state's emergency powers, military deployment authority, mass arrests, and criminalization of dissent are proportionate and lawful responses.
framings.emphasizes: Emergency legislation suspending constitutional rights, 365 arrests, potential military deployment, history of 2003 Gas War massacre killing 67, 'narco-terrorist' labeling of teachers and miners, Congress greenlighting armed forces
framings.downplays: Violence by some protesters (dynamite, Molotovs, attacks on convoys), genuine security challenges of 100+ road blockades, international support for Paz's government

gap_analysis: Missing: the banking sector's own perspective on operational disruption, security costs, and systemic risk exposure during prolonged closures. Missing: small business and informal economy impacts beyond headline class narratives—how street vendors, microfinance users, and remittance-dependent families experience bank closures. Missing: international creditor/IMF framing of fiscal discipline vs. social spending trade-offs that may have triggered austerity. Missing: regional labor union leadership positions and internal disagreements within protest movements themselves, rather than treating demonstrators as monolithic.
